content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Define the task, target output, and the observations available. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the result. 3. Run the code and compare actual and expected output. 4. Change one input or setting, repeat the experiment, and note what changed. 5. content_blocks.title: Practice reasoning
content_blocks.text: Metrics summarize different aspects of errors. Inspect the confusion matrix alongside aggregate scores to see which errors occur. For ranking and probability metrics, keep the problem definition, data selection, estimator configuration, and evaluation criterion explicit. When results are uncertain, compare a baseline and inspect examples rather than treating one metric as a complete explanation.

content_blocks.code:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report
y_true = [0, 0, 1, 1]
y_pred = [0, 1, 1, 1]
print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).tolist())
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run locally with Python 3 in the project virtual environment. Install the course-compatible dependencies with `python -m pip install scikit-learn numpy scipy pandas matplotlib joblib`. Save the snippet as `main.py` and run `python main.py`. This CodeLeaf content block documents a command; it does not execute Python inside the browser. Verify API compatibility against the installed Scikit-learn version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and fixed random seeds, rerun it, and change one input at a time. Use only synthetic or appropriately licensed data. Do not add credentials or private information.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Check input shapes, target alignment, data types, missing values, label order, and whether the expected output assumes a fixed random seed. Fit learned preprocessing only on training data, preferably inside a Pipeline. Do not select parameters by repeatedly looking at the final test set.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Ranking and Probability Metrics is part of Model Evaluation, Validation, and Selection. Define the task, inspect the inputs, choose a simple reference approach, and test the result on representative examples before drawing conclusions. Use the listed syllabus topics as a checklist, then complete the Try it yourself task. The goal is not to maximize a score at any cost; it is to build a reproducible, fit-for-purpose workflow whose evidence and limits are clear.

content.task: Try it yourself: use a small synthetic or built-in dataset to practice ranking and probability metrics. State the inputs, predicted outcome, assumptions, and one limitation; compare the result with a baseline or a manually traceable expectation where appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Accurately address the lesson topic and its listed syllabus subtopics.
Record the predicted and observed result or a clear manual trace.
State an assumption, failure mode, or limitation and how it was checked.
hints: Write down inputs, expected output, and assumptions before running code.
Keep data splitting, fitting, transformation, and evaluation steps explicit; use reproducible settings when randomness is involved.
Change one condition at a time and document whether the result supports the original hypothesis.
troubleshooting: Run in the project virtual environment and inspect `python -c "import sklearn; print(sklearn.__version__)"`.
If output differs, check package versions, fixed seeds, data order, and input shapes before changing the model.
If the code references a newer API, compare the installed-version API reference and use the supported equivalent rather than guessing.
Examples use toy or built-in data; they do not establish production accuracy or business impact.
